lessons.title: Brain overview
lessons.objective: Identify the brain as part of the central nervous system and describe how it receives, processes and sends information.
lessons.body: The brain works with the spinal cord as the central nervous system. It receives information from the senses and the body, processes it, and coordinates responses. Brain functions depend on networks of connected regions rather than one isolated 'control button'.
keyPoints: The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system.
Different regions have specialized roles and work together.
The model is a simplified learning diagram, not a medical scan.
lessons.check: What structures form the central nervous system?

lessons.title: Major parts and regions
lessons.objective: Compare the broad roles of the cerebrum, cerebellum and brainstem, and identify selected cortical and memory-related regions.
lessons.body: The cerebrum supports perception, voluntary movement, language, reasoning and many aspects of learning. The cerebellum helps coordinate movement, balance and motor learning. The brainstem connects the brain with the spinal cord and supports essential functions such as breathing and heart-rate regulation. These are broad summaries; each function involves interacting networks.
keyPoints: Cerebrum: perception, thinking, language and voluntary movement.
Cerebellum: coordination, balance and motor learning.
Brainstem: connection to spinal cord and essential automatic functions.
Hippocampus: important for forming and organizing new memories.
lessons.check: Which region is especially important for balance and movement coordination?

lessons.title: Neurons and synapses
lessons.objective: Label the cell body, dendrites, axon and axon terminals, and explain basic synaptic communication.
lessons.body: Neurons are specialized cells that communicate. Dendrites receive many incoming signals; the cell body contains the nucleus; the axon carries signals away from the cell body; and axon terminals communicate with another cell. At a chemical synapse, neurotransmitter molecules cross a tiny gap and bind to receptors on the receiving cell. This is a simplified overview of a more complex process.
keyPoints: The axon carries an electrical signal along the neuron.
At many synapses, chemical messengers carry information across a small gap.
Not all neurons or synapses are identical.
lessons.check: What is the name of the junction where one neuron communicates with another?

lessons.title: Memory and learning
lessons.objective: Describe memory as a network process and recognize the hippocampus as important in forming new memories.
lessons.body: Learning changes how neural networks respond. The hippocampus is important for forming and organizing many new memories, while long-term knowledge involves distributed networks across the brain. Practice, attention, sleep and prior knowledge can all influence learning. No single brain area stores every memory by itself.
keyPoints: The hippocampus contributes to forming many new memories.
Long-term memory depends on distributed brain networks.
Practice and retrieval help strengthen learning.
lessons.check: Does one small brain structure store every long-term memory?
lessons.answer: No. Memory relies on distributed networks; the hippocampus has an important role in forming many new memories.

lessons.title: The nervous system
lessons.objective: Distinguish the central and peripheral nervous systems and trace a basic sensory-response pathway.
lessons.body: The central nervous system includes the brain and spinal cord. The peripheral nervous system includes nerves and ganglia outside them. Sensory pathways carry information toward the central nervous system; motor pathways carry commands toward muscles and glands. Real pathways can involve several processing stages and feedback loops.
keyPoints: Central nervous system: brain and spinal cord.
Peripheral nervous system: nerves and ganglia outside the CNS.
Sensory information travels toward the CNS; motor output travels toward effectors.
lessons.check: Which system includes nerves outside the brain and spinal cord?

brainParts.name: Cerebrum
brainParts.summary: Largest major part; involved in perception, voluntary movement, language, thinking and learning.
brainParts.detail: Its outer cerebral cortex is folded and contains many networks involved in complex functions.

brainParts.name: Cerebellum
brainParts.summary: Helps coordinate movement, posture and balance; supports motor learning.
brainParts.detail: It fine-tunes movement using information from the body and other brain regions.

brainParts.name: Brainstem
brainParts.summary: Connects the brain to the spinal cord and helps regulate essential automatic functions.
brainParts.detail: Includes the midbrain, pons and medulla.

brainParts.name: Hippocampus
brainParts.summary: Important for forming and organizing many new memories.
brainParts.detail: It works with wider networks; it is not a single storage box for all memories.

islamicConnections.note: The verse invites reflection on travelling through the earth and learning from what is observed; it mentions hearts with which to reason and ears with which to hear. Use an institution-approved translation and tafsir for teaching.
These verses are commonly taught in connection with reading, knowledge and teaching. Present the passage as a spiritual and educational reflection, not as a technical explanation of brain anatomy.

The verse refers to people emerging from their mothers without knowledge and being given hearing, sight and hearts so that they may be grateful. Do not equate the verse's wording directly with a modern neuroscience diagram.

quiz.question: Which broad structure helps coordinate balance and movement?
quiz.explanation: The cerebellum helps coordinate movement, posture and balance.

quiz.question: Which neuron part commonly receives incoming signals?
quiz.explanation: Dendrites receive many incoming signals from other cells.

quiz.question: What is a synapse?
quiz.explanation: A synapse is a junction where a neuron communicates with another cell.

quiz.question: Which statement about memory is most accurate?
options: All memories are stored in one tiny region
Memory uses distributed networks; the hippocampus helps form many new memories
Memory does not change with learning
quiz.explanation: Memory involves multiple brain networks; the hippocampus is important for forming many new memories.

quiz.question: What structures form the central nervous system?
quiz.explanation: The central nervous system consists of the brain and spinal cord.
